title: Urinary tract infection in children (India, ISPN)
subject: paediatrics
setting: Primary care, paediatric outpatients, emergency department, ward
summary: Screen with dipstick and confirm by culture of a properly collected sample. Treat febrile UTI promptly with an oral third-generation cephalosporin or co-amoxiclav for 7 to 10 days, do an ultrasound for all, reserve MCU for selected children, and limit prophylaxis to high-grade VUR or recurrent UTI with bladder-bowel dysfunction.

sections.title: When to suspect
items: Fever for more than 48 hours without a focus in children under 24 months, or dysuria, frequency, urgency, abdominal or flank pain in older children. Infants may have only fever, vomiting, diarrhoea or poor weight gain.

Febrile UTI: temperature 38°C or more with a significant growth of a single uropathogen. Cystitis: dysuria, frequency, urgency and suprapubic tenderness without fever. Recurrent UTI: 2 episodes at any time in childhood.

Risk factors: vesicoureteric reflux, bladder-bowel dysfunction (urgency, frequency, holding, incontinence, constipation), previous UTI, and congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract (obstruction, phimosis, labial adhesions, stones).
E. coli causes more than 70% of cases; fungal UTI occurs with immunosuppression, ICU stay, prolonged antibiotics or indwelling catheters.

sections.title: Collect urine and confirm
items: Toilet-trained: midstream clean-catch after washing the genital area. Non-toilet-trained but stable: try clean-catch first, then catheterisation or suprapubic aspiration if unsuccessful. Sick infants: catheter or suprapubic aspiration. Never culture a bag sample.
Process urine within 30 minutes of collection. Send culture before the first antibiotic dose.

Screen with dipstick (leucocyte esterase or nitrite; sensitivity 84%, specificity 88%) or fresh urine microscopy: leucocyturia is 10 or more white cells/mm3 uncentrifuged or more than 5 per high-power field centrifuged; bacteriuria is 1 or more organisms per oil-immersion field.

Significant growth of a single uropathogen: 10^3 CFU/mL or more by suprapubic aspiration, 10^4 CFU/mL or more by catheter, 10^4 to 10^5 CFU/mL or more by clean-catch. Leucocyturia is not required when culture is positive with symptoms.
Do not culture urine from asymptomatic children, and do not treat asymptomatic bacteriuria.

sections.title: Antibiotics
items: Start as soon as possible, preferably within 48 to 72 hours of fever onset, to limit kidney scarring.

Febrile UTI: third-generation cephalosporin or co-amoxiclav. Oral treatment is preferred for all except infants under 2 months, severely ill children, and those unable to take oral drugs, who need IV therapy.
Duration: 7 to 10 days for febrile UTI; 3 to 7 days orally for cystitis in adolescents, with a first-generation cephalosporin (cephalexin, cefadroxil) or co-amoxiclav.

Oral doses (IAP): cefixime 10 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses; amoxicillin or co-amoxiclav 30 to 50 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses; cephalexin 30 to 50 mg/kg/day in 3 divided doses; cefadroxil 30 to 40 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses.

IV doses (IAP): ceftriaxone 75 to 100 mg/kg/day in 1 to 2 doses; cefotaxime 100 mg/kg/day in 2 to 3 doses; amikacin 10 to 15 mg/kg/day (once daily is effective); gentamicin 5 to 6 mg/kg/day in 1 to 2 doses.

Change antibiotics only for clinical failure, not for a mismatched sensitivity report in a child who is improving. If there is no response, do an urgent kidney ultrasound and adjust to culture. Response is judged clinically; repeat culture is not needed.

sections.title: Imaging after UTI (ISPN 2023)
items: Kidney, ureter and bladder ultrasound after an episode of UTI in all children.
Micturating cystourethrogram (MCU), usually 2 to 3 weeks after treatment, only if: abnormal ultrasound, recurrent UTI, or UTI caused by a non-E. coli organism under 2 years.
No acute-phase DMSA scan. Late DMSA 4 to 6 months after UTI only for recurrent UTI or high-grade (grade 3 to 5) VUR, to detect scarring.
Screen siblings under 3 years of a child with primary VUR by ultrasound only.

sections.title: Prevent recurrence
items: Antibiotic prophylaxis only for high-grade (grade 3 to 5) VUR, or recurrent febrile UTI with bladder-bowel dysfunction; it may be considered in infants with low-grade VUR. Not for a normal urinary tract, and not for antenatal hydronephrosis awaiting evaluation.

Prophylaxis once daily: cotrimoxazole 1 to 2 mg/kg of trimethoprim or nitrofurantoin 1 to 2 mg/kg (first line over 3 months); cephalexin 10 mg/kg in young infants. Avoid cotrimoxazole under 3 months and in G6PD deficiency; do not use co-amoxiclav or other broad-spectrum drugs.
Stop prophylaxis after 2 years of age once toilet trained, without bladder-bowel dysfunction, and free of febrile UTI for the preceding year.
Evaluate every toilet-trained child for bladder-bowel dysfunction and treat with urotherapy (regular voiding, adequate fluids, good posture) and laxatives for constipation.
Cranberry products may be used for recurrent UTI with a normal urinary tract. Circumcision can be offered to boys at risk (high-grade VUR or recurrent UTI).
Surgical reimplantation (or endoscopic bulking agent, less effective) only for recurrent breakthrough febrile UTI on prophylaxis despite managing bladder-bowel dysfunction.

sections.title: Follow-up
items: Aim for sustained resolution of fever and symptoms; check urinalysis during later febrile illnesses in children with risk factors.
High-grade VUR or reflux nephropathy: growth, BP, proteinuria and kidney function at each visit, and periodic ultrasound for kidney growth. Repeat DMSA only after recurrent UTI.
Repeat cystography to document resolution is not routinely needed; if required, 4 to 8 years after diagnosis.
After severe, complicated or recurrent UTI (IAP): BP every 6 to 12 months and kidney function yearly.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Culturing bag or urobag samples, or delaying transport to the laboratory.
Using the old threshold of 10^5 CFU/mL for catheter or suprapubic samples and missing true UTI in infants.
Delaying antibiotics beyond 48 to 72 hours of fever while awaiting culture.
Routine MCU and DMSA for every first UTI.
Long-term prophylaxis for a normal urinary tract, which breeds resistance without benefit.

drugs.name: Cefixime
drugs.dose: 10 mg/kg/day orally in 2 divided doses for 7 to 10 days
drugs.notes: Good empirical oral choice for febrile UTI.

drugs.name: Co-amoxiclav (amoxicillin-clavulanate)
drugs.dose: 30 to 50 mg/kg/day (amoxicillin) orally in 2 divided doses

drugs.name: Cephalexin
drugs.dose: Treatment 30 to 50 mg/kg/day in 3 divided doses; prophylaxis 10 mg/kg once daily
drugs.notes: Cystitis in adolescents; prophylaxis in young infants.

drugs.name: Ceftriaxone
drugs.dose: 75 to 100 mg/kg/day IV in 1 to 2 doses
drugs.notes: Infants under 2 months, sick or vomiting children.

drugs.name: Amikacin
drugs.notes: Alternative parenteral agent; monitor renal function.

drugs.name: Cotrimoxazole (prophylaxis)
drugs.dose: 1 to 2 mg/kg of trimethoprim once daily
drugs.notes: Over 3 months; avoid in G6PD deficiency.
